title: The claim you can check
summary: A 90 second demo talk on the gate circuit with one claim tested live, and a sorting game: which claims can you check yourself, and which need someone's word?
materials: the AND and OR circuit from Build

steps.title: Two kinds of claims
steps.body:
A claim is a sentence that says something is so. This week's game is noticing that claims come in two kinds.

Some claims you can check yourself, today, with your own hands: the LED only lights when both buttons are pressed. Press the buttons and watch. The claim survives the check or it does not, and you never had to trust anybody.

Other claims you have to take on someone's word: the sun is about 150 million kilometres away. It happens to be true, but you cannot stretch a tape measure to the sun. You are trusting the people and the instruments that measured it. Trusting is fine, as long as you notice you are doing it, and notice whose word you are taking.

The philosophy question of the week sits right under this: how do you know something is true? Keep your answer simmering while you work. Your talk ends with it.

Voice rules, the same three as always: speak to the back wall, pause after the sentence that matters most, and look at one person per sentence.

steps.title: Sort the claims
steps.body:
Draw two columns on the whiteboard: check it myself, and take someone's word. Say each claim below out loud, then write it in a column and say why it goes there.

1. This LED only lights when both buttons are pressed.
2. The sun is about 150 million kilometres away.
3. Two buttons can make four different press patterns.
4. The chip on the micro:bit holds billions of transistors.
5. Our multimeter beeps when a path is complete.
6. Sharks lived on Earth before trees existed.
7. Ten switches can show more than a thousand patterns.
8. From a pile of 20, nobody in the world can beat perfect play at the 21 game.

Some of these are sneaky. Number 7 sounds like something to take on trust, but you counted the doubling yourself in Think this week, so it moved columns the moment you did the math. Number 8 you can check against any grown-up you can find. For every claim that lands in the trust column, ask the follow-up out loud: whose word, and how did they come to know it?
checklist: All eight claims landed in a column, each with a reason said out loud
At least one claim moved columns after a second thought
Claim 1 got checked for real on the circuit, all four button ways
For one trust-column claim, I said whose word I am taking and how they might know

steps.title: Prepare the demo talk
steps.body:
Ninety seconds, circuit on the table, camera rolling. The shape of the talk:

Open with the claim, said plainly: this light only comes on when both buttons are pressed.

Then the check, narrated while your hands do it: neither button, one, the other, both. Four presses, four results, and the claim survives in front of everyone.

Then one sentence on why: the buttons sit in a chain, and current needs the whole chain.

Close with your answer to the question of the week: how do you know something is true? You just showed one way with your own hands. Say it in your own words.

Practise twice with a timer. The pause goes right after the both-buttons press, when the LED comes on: let the light do the talking for a second before you do.
checklist: Under 90 seconds, twice in a row
The claim comes first, before any wires get explained
All four button combinations shown to the camera
Ends with my own answer to how do you know something is true

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the demo talk in one take: circuit on the table, both hands in frame, whole face visible when you look up.
